prompt.context: Your client is a large pharmaceutical drug company working on a vaccine for chicken pox. The vaccine needs to pass three phases of testing to be approved by the FDA. It has just completed the second phase and the client is asking your help to decide if they should fund the third phase. The third phase would last 2 years, cost $300M, and results from previous phases indicate the vaccine has a 95% chance of approval. We would be able to start producing vaccine immediately following approval.
prompt.question: Should the client fund the third and final phase of testing for the chicken pox vaccine? Go or No-Go?

clarifying_info.a: We are only worried about the US market in this case.

clarifying_info.q: What form does the vaccine take?
clarifying_info.a: The vaccine is a one-time pill.

clarifying_info.q: What is the US population and age distribution?
clarifying_info.a: Assume US population is 300M and uniformly distributed from age 0-75 (as many people enter population as leave every year).

clarifying_info.q: What portion of the population would need the vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: [Hand candidate Exhibit 1 — cumulative distribution of chicken pox exposure by age.]

clarifying_info.q: How long would it take to vaccinate the existing population?
clarifying_info.a: It is estimated that it would take 3 years to vaccinate the existing population.
[Hand candidate Exhibit 2 — parents' willingness to pay.] Have the candidate estimate the optimal price from the exhibit.
Distribution: $1.50; Production: $2.50; SG&A: $5.00. The $300M phase-three cost covers everything else (plant setup, etc.) and can be spread over the 2 years of testing.
The vaccine will not be patented.

clarifying_info.q: Are other companies developing a competing vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: No other companies have started formal testing of a vaccine. Other companies would have to undergo the same three-phase testing series to gain FDA approval.

clarifying_info.q: How long do phases 1 and 2 take and cost?
clarifying_info.a: Phases 1 and 2 combined take 3 years and cost $200M.

exhibits.title: Cumulative Distribution of Chicken Pox Exposure
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the cumulative percentage of the population that has been exposed to (and thus already had) chicken pox, plotted against age from 0 to 21+. The curve rises from 0% at birth, reaches approximately 50% around age 6, and approaches 100% by age 18.

data.key_points: ~50% infected by age 6; ~100% infected by age 18

exhibits.title: Parent's Willingness to Pay
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the percentage of parents willing to purchase the vaccine at various price points. The curve slopes downward as price increases.

data.key_points: ~100% willing at $10; ~75% willing at $30; ~50% willing at $35; ~25% willing at $40+

framework: Define the decision: go/no-go to fund Phase 3 based on expected NPV vs. $300M investment
Market sizing: estimate addressable US population needing the vaccine (existing unvaccinated + annual newborns)
Revenue: determine optimal price using willingness-to-pay curve and compute annual revenue
Cost structure: per-unit variable costs plus Phase 3 investment (sunk costs from Phases 1-2 excluded)
Financial model: build year-by-year cash flow table and assess NPV at a reasonable pharma hurdle rate
Risk adjustment: account for 5% probability of Phase 3 failure
Competitive analysis: assess whether competitors will enter and how that affects long-run profitability
Recommendation: synthesize NPV and competitive moat into a clear go/no-go

questions.prompt: How large is the existing population that needs the vaccine?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 1 shows ~100% exposure by age 18, meaning only children under 18 who have not yet had chicken pox need the vaccine. The curve is roughly linear 0-18, so on average ~50% of the 0-18 cohort has already been exposed. US population is 300M uniform 0-75, so each age has 4M people. Ages 0-17 = 18 age-cohorts x 4M = 72M total; approximately half (50%) still susceptible = 36M existing unvaccinated. Exhibit 2 at a $30 price shows 75% willingness to purchase, so 36M x 75% = 27M doses over the 3-year rollout, or 9M per year.

math.setup: Each age cohort = 300M / 75 = 4M people. Ages 0-18 = 18 cohorts. Half are susceptible on average (triangular area under exposure curve). 75% of parents willing at $30.
math.answer: 9M doses/year for 3 years from existing population

questions.prompt: How many doses are sold each year from newborns going forward?
questions.guidance: In steady state, 4M babies are born per year (300M / 75). At $30 price, 75% of parents will vaccinate, giving 3M doses/year in perpetuity starting at Year 3.

questions.prompt: What is the optimal price and what is the profit per pill?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 2 shows a demand curve. At $30 approximately 75% of parents are willing to pay, which maximizes revenue (price x quantity). Total per-pill variable cost = $1.50 (distribution) + $2.50 (production) + $5.00 (SG&A) = $9.00. Profit per pill = $30 - $9 = $21.

math.setup: Revenue per pill = Price x % willing. Compare price points from Exhibit 2. Variable cost = $1.50 + $2.50 + $5.00.
steps: At $30: revenue index = 30 x 75% = 22.5 (highest on curve)

questions.prompt: Build a year-by-year cash flow model and assess whether NPV is positive.
questions.guidance: Phase 3 testing spans Years 1-2 ($150M cost each year, no revenue). Vaccine launched in Year 3. Existing population rollout provides 9M doses/year for 3 years (Years 3-5). Annual newborn cohort provides 3M doses/year from Year 3 onward. Candidate should show revenue, variable costs, and net profit per year, then note NPV is highly positive at any reasonable pharma hurdle rate. Must mention the 5% failure probability (reduces expected NPV).

math.setup: Revenue = doses x $30. Variable costs = doses x $9. Phase 3 cost = $300M split over 2 years = $150M/year. Values in millions.
steps: Year 3: (9M + 3M) = 12M doses; Revenue = 12M x $30 = $360M; Variable cost = 12M x $9 = $108M; Net = $252M
Year 6+: 3M doses/year (newborns only); Revenue = $90M; Cost = $27M; Net = $63M/year
Total net Years 1-5: -150 -150 +252 +252 +252 = +$456M before discounting, plus $63M/year perpetuity
math.answer: NPV is strongly positive at any reasonable discount rate; recommend GO

brainstorming.prompt: What factors from the competitive landscape should influence the go/no-go decision?

categories.name: Barriers to entry
ideas: Competitors must complete same three-phase FDA testing process
Phases 1 and 2 take 3 years and cost $200M — high time and capital barrier
No other companies have started formal testing, giving a minimum 3-year head start

categories.name: Market window
ideas: 3-year exclusive window captures the entire existing unvaccinated population (27M doses)
Competitors entering after Year 5 can only compete for the annual newborn segment (3M/year)
Small annual newborn market may not justify $200M+ investment for a late entrant

categories.name: Competitor incentives
ideas: Late entrant faces sunk Phase 1-2 costs we have already incurred — these are not sunk for them
Annual newborn market revenues ($63M/year at full capture) may never recoup their testing investment
Rational competitors likely conclude the market is not worth entering after we have first-mover advantage

categories.name: Sunk costs clarification
ideas: Phases 1-2 cost ($200M) is sunk for us and should not affect our go/no-go decision
However, it is a real future cost for potential competitors, deterring entry

categories.name: Risk factors
ideas: 5% probability Phase 3 fails — adjust expected NPV accordingly
No patent protection means price competition if competitors do enter
Regulatory changes could alter vaccine approval timelines

recommendation: Recommend GO: fund the third phase of testing
Expected NPV is strongly positive — even risk-adjusted for 5% failure probability, the project generates hundreds of millions in net present value
The natural 3-year competitive moat from FDA testing requirements means the client can capture the entire existing unvaccinated population (27M doses) without competition
risks: 5% probability of Phase 3 failure results in loss of $300M investment and $200M sunk in prior phases
If a competitor begins Phase 1 testing simultaneously, the competitive window shrinks (though they still cannot enter until Year 6 at earliest)
No patent protection exposes the newborn segment to future price competition
next_steps: Fund Phase 3 immediately to begin the 2-year testing clock
Plan manufacturing scale-up to be ready for immediate post-approval production
Develop market access and pricing strategy; set price at $30 to maximize revenue
Monitor competitor pipeline for any new FDA filings
